prose.kicker: Nobody Played The Guy Next Door
prose.title: Eric Martel Beat Everybody. Matt Gerardi Beat Nobody.
prose.dek: Every matchup on the board skipped its own division, Ryan Bousquet's Bo Nix put up the loudest number in the league, and the race at the bottom of MAKE IT RAIN didn't move an inch.

paragraphs: Eric Martel went {{f.team.0005.week_allplay}} against the field this week, and the outcome was basically decided before most owners had finished setting their lineups. Ja'Marr Chase went for {{f.player.ja-marr-chase.score}} on Thursday night, and Martel spent the rest of the weekend just watching the number hold up like a lead he never had to defend. He finished {{f.team.0005.vs_avg}} over his own average — {{f.team.0005.week_rank_own}} — and left almost nothing behind: {{f.team.0005.left_on_bench}} points stranded on a bench that never mattered.

Ryan Bousquet's week broke later and louder. Bo Nix waited to go to work, and when he was done he'd put up the single best line in the league: {{f.star.line}}, good for {{f.star.score}} points on a card that had been averaging {{f.star.prior_avg}}. Bousquet turned it into the largest margin of the week, hanging {{f.game.10.margin}} on Matt Gerardi — {{f.game.10.margin_rank}} — and posting {{f.team.0001.week_rank_own}} in the process.

Gerardi's weekend never had a chance to turn. He went {{f.team.0003.week_allplay}} against the field — {{f.team.0003.week_rank_own}}, {{f.team.0003.season_pf_rank}} — and {{f.team.0003.could_have_won}}: the best lineup on his bench still finished behind every score that beat him, three times over. LEGION OF BOOM has an owner sitting on {{f.team.0004.season_pf_rank}} and an owner sitting on {{f.team.0003.season_pf_rank}}, and this week both ends of that split got louder.

The wire moved {{f.wire.adds}} bodies this week and {{f.wire.trades}} trades actually went through. The best of the pickups was Derrick Whitman's {{f.wire.best_add}} — started and cashed the same week he claimed it — and he wasn't the only one who got it right: six of the eight adds that cleared double-digit points actually found their way into a starting lineup. Ryan Bousquet is the hottest team in the league over the last three weeks at {{f.mo.hot}}; Keith Creelman is the coldest at {{f.mo.cold}}, a stretch ugly enough that his own group chat has stopped asking him what happened and started just sending condolences.

captions.t.performers: Five different quarterbacks in the top ten, which is what this format looks like on a week nobody's defense showed up.
captions.t.pickups: Six of the eight adds that cleared double-digit points actually got started; the other two just sat and watched, same as usual.

paragraphs: Eighteen games on the board, and not one of them was played against a division rival — the whole slate skipped the neighborhood this week. The headline is Ryan Bousquet turning Bo Nix loose on Matt Gerardi for the loudest number of the season, but that's just the marquee act on a slate that also produced a perfect week for Eric Martel, a full-on identity crisis for Brian Cutting, and a finish so tight the last game of the week came down to a field goal's worth of points. Here's the whole board, biggest matchup first.

Start with the Game of the Week, because the rest of the league did too: Ryan Bousquet {{f.game.01.margin}}, {{f.game.01.margin_rank}}, over Brian Cutting — the same Brian Cutting who owns {{f.team.0004.season_pf_rank}}. {{f.team.0001.best_player}} was simply the better story than {{f.team.0004.best_player}}, Cutting finished {{f.team.0004.vs_avg}} under his own average, and {{f.team.0004.could_have_won}}. The league's best scorer got run over by the league's best week, and the record book will file it as a Cutting loss when it should file it as a Bousquet week.

Cutting didn't have to wait long to answer, though — his only win of the week came against a Bear Dunn team already having {{f.team.0009.week_rank_own}}. {{f.game.02.margin}} decided it, and Cutting didn't need to be good to get there; Dunn's card was just worse. Call it a win manufactured entirely by the other guy's week.

Then Eric Mannila closed out a genuinely rough week for Cutting's roster, {{f.game.03.margin}}, behind {{f.team.0011.best_player}}. Cutting's best player showed up again and it still wasn't enough — {{f.team.0004.could_have_won}}. Two losses bookending one gift of a win, and LEGION OF BOOM's top seed heads into next week having proven a lot less than his record suggests.

Back to Bousquet, whose other blowout, {{f.game.04.margin}}, buried Josh Martel under Bo Nix's number a second time. {{f.team.0007.best_player}} had a monster night of his own and it still wasn't the best individual number in the building — that was Bo Nix's, and it wasn't close. Martel's bench told the harder story: {{f.burn.benched}} sat behind {{f.burn.started}}, the single biggest points left on any bench all week, and whether that was the wrong call or just a quiet night for the guy who sat is something even the verdict column calls unclear.

Bear Dunn's second win, also over Josh Martel, came by the tightest margin of his week — {{f.game.05.margin}}. This is the one where the math actually turns: put {{f.burn.benched}} in for {{f.burn.started}} and Martel wins it outright. He didn't, and whatever you want to call that bench call, the outcome of a completely different game hinged on it.

Derrick Whitman's closest win of the week, {{f.game.06.margin}}, came off {{f.team.0002.best_player}} — a season high — against a Shawn Blake card that never got out of the mud. Whitman had his own quiet miscue on the bench that week ({{f.team.0002.left_on_bench}} points left stranded, the table below has the full breakdown), and it still didn't matter. Blake's whole week fits in one number: {{f.team.0010.vs_avg}} under his own average, in a loss decided by less than a converted first down.

Then Eric Martel found Shawn Blake a second time and buried him by {{f.game.07.margin}}, one of the widest margins of the week outside the Bousquet-Gerardi demolition. {{f.team.0005.best_player}} did the damage. Blake has now run into both of the league's hottest cards in the same slate — bad scheduling luck stacked directly on top of a bad week.

Whitman's other win, over Keith Creelman, was tighter — {{f.game.08.margin}} — off the same {{f.team.0002.best_player}} line. Creelman's best number, {{f.team.0008.best_player}}, kept it competitive and nothing else. His week did not get better from here.

It got worse two games later, when Eric Martel ran his week to {{f.team.0005.week_allplay}} by putting Creelman away a second time, {{f.game.09.margin}} — the second-largest margin of the week, bigger even than his own win over Blake. {{f.team.0005.best_player}} did the heavy lifting again. Creelman is now sitting on the wrong end of the coldest stretch in the league, and it's starting to show up in more than one column.

Which brings us back to the number of the week: Bousquet over Gerardi, {{f.game.10.margin}}, {{f.game.10.margin_rank}}. {{f.team.0001.best_player}} did what it did, Gerardi's best player, {{f.team.0003.best_player}}, was never in the conversation, and {{f.team.0003.could_have_won}}. There was no version of this one that ends differently.

Chris Klingenberg's best win of the week, over Derrick Whitman, actually came down to the bench: {{f.game.11.margin_rank}} in margin, and Whitman left {{f.team.0002.left_on_bench}} points on his own bench in a game he lost by less than that. {{f.team.0002.best_player}} actually outscored {{f.team.0012.best_player}} head to head, and Klingenberg won anyway — {{f.game.11.margin}} — because Whitman {{f.team.0002.could_have_won}}, and that's the real headline: not the player matchup, but a lineup that never got tight.

Eric Martel's third win, closing out his perfect week, came against that same Klingenberg team, {{f.game.12.margin}}. {{f.team.0005.best_player}} was the story again — that's what a card running {{f.team.0005.vs_avg}} over its own baseline does to a good team on a good week. Klingenberg's own ceiling this week was {{f.team.0012.ceiling_rank}}, which tells you exactly how good his roster actually was; it just ran into the best week in the league.

Bear Dunn closed his own week the way it opened, beating Matt Gerardi by {{f.game.13.margin}} behind {{f.team.0009.best_player}}. Two wins, two forgettable scores, and a division record that says a lot more about Dunn's season than either one of them did.

Eric Mannila's best win of the week, {{f.game.14.margin}}, came at Josh Martel's expense and off {{f.team.0011.best_player}} — the same card that carried him to {{f.team.0011.week_rank_own}}. Martel had the single best player on the field, {{f.team.0007.best_player}}, and lost anyway — his third loss in three games. The same swap from earlier still applies here: {{f.burn.covers_margin}}.

Brian Cross's first win, over Shawn Blake, went by {{f.game.15.margin}} on the back of {{f.team.0006.best_player}}, a season high. It was {{f.team.0006.week_rank_own}}, and it came against a Blake team that just wrapped up a week that ended in three straight losses by a combined margin nobody wants to add up.

Cross's second win, over Keith Creelman, was wider — {{f.game.16.margin}} — off the same {{f.team.0006.best_player}} line. Creelman's card, led again by {{f.team.0008.best_player}}, simply didn't have the depth behind it. Three losses on the week for Creelman, and the pattern is no longer hiding.

Eric Mannila's third win, over Matt Gerardi, {{f.game.17.margin}}, was the least competitive of his week and the most predictable result on the board — a Gride roster with nothing left to give by its third meeting of the weekend. Mannila quietly won every game he played this week; nobody's talking about that, because nobody's talking about anything except the top of the standings.

The week ended exactly the way a good week should: on its closest game. Chris Klingenberg beat Brian Cross by {{f.game.18.margin}}, {{f.game.18.margin_rank}}, behind {{f.team.0012.best_player}}. Cross's own {{f.team.0006.best_player}} nearly got there. Nobody on either side left a winning swap on the bench — this one just came down to whose good decisions scored more.

gameNotes.g.1: Brian Cutting brought {{f.team.0004.season_pf_rank}} into the biggest game of the week, and Bo Nix simply outscored him. Cutting was under his own average; Bousquet was nowhere near his ceiling and didn't need to be. History will log this as a Cutting loss. It should log it as a Bousquet week.
gameNotes.g.2: Brian Cutting's only win of the week, and it says more about Bear Dunn's week than his own. Dunn was already having {{f.team.0009.week_rank_own}}, and Cutting didn't need to play well to beat it. Neither roster was good here; one of them was simply less bad.
gameNotes.g.3: Cutting's second loss of the week is the one that actually stings — {{f.team.0004.best_player}} showed up again and it still wasn't enough. Eric Mannila didn't have to be great, just present. A card that will win plenty of weeks it doesn't deserve to didn't get one of them here.
gameNotes.g.4: Josh Martel's week in one page: {{f.team.0007.best_player}} was excellent and still not the best individual score in the building, and the biggest bench swing of the week sits right below it — genuinely unclear whether it cost him anything or was just a quiet night for the guy who sat. Bousquet's number did the rest.
gameNotes.g.5: The game that actually turns on the bench call, whatever you want to label it. Martel had the ceiling to win this one outright and left it on his own roster before Dunn ever had to be good. Dunn was not good. He did not need to be.
gameNotes.g.6: The tightest of Derrick Whitman's three wins, and the one where Shawn Blake's week is most visible — well under his own average, in a game decided by less than a field goal's worth of points. Whitman's bench was deep enough to survive its own quiet miscue.
gameNotes.g.7: One of Martel's two biggest wins of the week, and Blake's second loss of the slate. There's no lineup call to blame here — Blake simply drew two of the hottest cards in the league in the same week and lost both by a lot.
gameNotes.g.8: Whitman's closer win, and Keith Creelman's first loss of what turns into a long week. Creelman's best player kept the score respectable. Nothing else on his roster showed up to help him.
gameNotes.g.9: Martel's biggest win of the week, and the number that pushed his own week to its final shape. Creelman's card had no counter for a roster this hot; nobody's did.
gameNotes.g.10: The biggest number of the week, attached to {{f.team.0003.week_rank_own}} for Matt Gerardi. Bousquet's ceiling was never in danger. Gerardi's best lineup available still finishes behind what actually beat him — there was no version of this one that goes the other way.
gameNotes.g.11: The one game this week where the bench genuinely decided the outcome. Whitman left real points behind unused. He {{f.team.0002.could_have_won}}, and that's the entire story — not Klingenberg's decisions, but his own.
gameNotes.g.12: Klingenberg's ceiling was {{f.team.0012.ceiling_rank}}, and he still lost by a wide margin, which says everything about how good Martel's week actually was. A flawless Klingenberg card beats most weeks in this league. It did not beat this one.
gameNotes.g.13: The less dramatic half of Dunn's doubleheader over Gerardi — same result, uglier number, and no change at the bottom of LEGION OF BOOM.
gameNotes.g.14: Mannila's best win of his week, and Josh Martel's third loss in three games — despite fielding, again, the single best player on the field. A team can lead the box score and still lose the week if the rest of the roster doesn't show up with him.
gameNotes.g.15: Brian Cross's week starts turning here, on the back of a receiver having his best game of the season. Blake's card, already cold, gets colder.
gameNotes.g.16: Cross's second win of the day, wider than his first, and Creelman's third loss of the week. By the end of the slate Creelman's card had stopped looking unlucky and started looking like a pattern.
gameNotes.g.17: The most lopsided of Mannila's three wins and the least surprising result of the entire week — Gerardi's roster had already proven twice over it had nothing left to give.
gameNotes.g.18: The closest game of the week, decided at the very end of the slate. No bad bench call on either side — just two good rosters, one very small gap, and Klingenberg's card being a fraction of a point better where it counted.

paragraphs: Read the four division leaders next to their division records and the tension in this format shows up fast. {{f.div.dog-pound-4-life.leader}} holds DOG POUND 4 LIFE despite a division record of {{f.team.0001.div_record}} — he's winning the league and losing his own neighborhood. Bear Dunn is the one actually doing damage inside it, {{f.team.0009.div_record}}, and still sits behind him on the overall math.

ICE UP SON! is the strangest of the four: {{f.div.ice-up-son.leader}} leads a division where all three teams sit at {{f.team.0005.div_record}} against each other. Nobody inside that group has separated from anybody else — the bid is being decided entirely by what each of them does to the other eight teams outside it, which is exactly backwards from how a division race is supposed to work.

LEGION OF BOOM is the one division that actually looks like a division. {{f.div.legion-of-boom.leader}} is unbeaten inside it at {{f.team.0004.div_record}}, and it's propping up a record that would otherwise read as ordinary — his week off the field was bad, his week inside his own group has been perfect all year. Matt Gerardi is the mirror image at the bottom, {{f.team.0003.div_record}}, and this week did nothing to change that story.

MAKE IT RAIN is the fourth automatic bid, and it belongs, for now, to a losing record. {{f.div.make-it-rain.leader}} leads it at a division mark that is the best of a genuinely bad group — Chris Klingenberg is right behind him even after {{f.team.0012.week_rank_own}}, and Keith Creelman, mired in the coldest three-week stretch anybody in this league is currently riding at {{f.mo.cold}}, is closer to the top of this division than his overall record has any business being. Whoever wins MAKE IT RAIN is going to back into a bid nobody else wanted badly enough to take from them.

Zoom out and the all-play table tells a cleaner story than any of the four division races do. Ryan Bousquet is the hottest team in the league over the last three weeks, {{f.mo.hot}}, and it's backed by real production — {{f.team.0001.season_pf_rank}}. Brian Cutting still sits on {{f.team.0004.season_pf_rank}} despite the week he just had, which is what a good September buys a bad October. And at the other end, Matt Gerardi is sitting on {{f.team.0003.season_pf_rank}}, and it isn't a slump anymore. This deep into the season, it's a pattern, and the results back it up every single week.

captions.t.standings: Match the Record column against the Div column before you decide who is actually in trouble — this week they disagree almost everywhere.
